invideo uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create full scenes in one prompt

“We’re really impressed by how fast and accurate this new model is. The outputs retain an amazing level of detail, and the model does a great job of making only the changes we ask for while keeping everything else consistent. We’re excited to use it for character and scene replacements, as well as other creative workflows.” – Numan Khan, Creative Specialist, Krea.

Krea uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash for their creative workflows, from character to scene replacements

"Gemini Omni 1.2 fits the way our teams work. Draft mode lets us iterate concepts in minutes, then render in 4K for TV-ready AI dramas. Text stays crisp across frames, characters look and sound real, and the speed keeps production moving. Now that it is generally available, we can bring this quality to over 100M Picsart creators." – Narek Hayrapetyan, Head of Product and Partnerships, Picsart.

Picsart uses Gemini 1.2 Flash to iterate concepts in minutes

Runway empowers creatives with advanced AI video tools to produce high-quality content. For organizations, Runway’s enterprise solutions deliver robust collaborative tools to scale professional production. Here is what they created with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash.

Runway uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to produce and scale high-quality content

Product and listing videos at catalog scale

Retailers and marketplaces use Gemini Omni to turn the photos they already have into short product spins, lifestyle clips, try-on videos, and video ads.

“Photoroom turns product photos into video ads that sell in minutes. We chose Gemini Omni Flash to power our Video Ad Maker and Product Animator because it balances quality, speed and cost. Version 1.2 brings 15-second videos, a top user request. With general availability and SLAs, we can rely on it in production for our sellers and enterprise customers.” - Matt Rouif, CEO and Co-founder, Photoroom.

Photoroom uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to power their Video Ad Maker and Product Animator

“QuickFrame AI helps marketers and business owners create, edit, and launch professional-quality ads for CTV and social in minutes. With Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash now supporting 15-second video generations at 1080p, users can create a complete CTV ad in a single generation, making TV ad creation simpler for businesses of all sizes.” - Richard Girges, Chief Technology Officer, QuickFrame AI.

QuickFrame AI uses Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash to create complete CTV ads in a single generation

Create in Gemini for business, Google Vids and build with the API

Coming soon to Gemini, business users will be able to create a short video from a prompt or a product photo, right in the chat. In Google Vids, teams can combine generated clips with avatars, music and voiceover to create product explainers, teasers, social posts and sales pitches. Businesses can also embed the capabilities of Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash into their applications and agents via the API.

Get started with Gemini Omni

We'll keep improving Gemini Omni based on your feedback, so tell us what you build.

  • For business users: Try it in Google Vids; coming soon to Gemini for business

  • For developers: Try it in the Google Cloud console, build with the API, and see the pricing

entries.content:
Ivan Nardini

AI Developer Relations Engineer

Anant Nawalgaria

Group Product Manager & Sr. Staff Engineer

Every day, more and more people are using coding agents like Google Antigravity and OpenCode to complete software engineering tasks. But those tools need instructions to operate and their output is only as good as the inputs they get. By utilizing agent skills that direct the agents through building, testing, and deploying code, developers have a powerful way to automate their workflows. 

But most skills are written manually, so it’s hard to know which instructions are effective without assessing their output.

To measure the effectiveness of our skills, we ran OpenCode with Gemini 3.8 Flash on tasks from Terminal-Bench 2.0, a public benchmark. The results were inconclusive: with our baseline skill, the agent passed about two-thirds of its attempts, but the outcome was about the same even without the skill. We needed better results.

To achieve them, we turned to AlphaEvolve, which optimizes skills the way it optimizes code: Gemini proposes a new version, an evaluator scores it, and the search retains the higher-scoring version. And with Harbor, that evaluator can be a real coding agent working on real tasks. We saw improvements of 5% with just a few iterations with alphaevolve

This is how you can build the same loop:

  • Treat the skill as the program: AlphaEvolve can rewrite your skill's text.

  • Let the agent judge: Harbor runs the agent with the skill on real tasks.

  • Make the score trustworthy: Compare each version to the baseline skill and run them both at the same time.

  • Check the winner on unseen tasks: Save some tasks the search never sees for your final check.

Treat the skill as the program

AlphaEvolve is designed to advance the code between two markers in a seed program. Skills are SKILL.md files with names, descriptions, and markdown instructions, so we put their text between the markers and let Gemini rewrite them:

AlphaEvolve operates in Google Cloud and doesn’t run your code. Its feedback is the scores and notes your evaluator sends back about what "better" means.

Image 1. AlphaEvolve proposes a skill, Harbor runs the agent with it next to the baseline skill, and the score and notes go back to AlphaEvolve.

Let the agent judge

Harbor runs agents on benchmark tasks, with each trial in its own container. We ran it on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) with one pod per trial, and a single search ran thousands of agent trials.

For each candidate, the evaluator returns a score for passes and failures, as well as short notes on tasks that failed or timed-out. AlphaEvolve then sends those notes to Gemini for the next version.

Make the score trustworthy

Agent scores can be noisy. In one of our early runs on the same benchmark, our model’s latency explained much of the variance in candidate scores. With each candidate running next to the baseline skill on the same tasks at the same time, their scores are the difference.

Check the winner on unseen tasks

The best skills read differently than the baseline, which is a careful checklist: read first, reproduce the failure, and work in small verified steps. AlphaEvolve's version is a protocol built around the time limit:

What we learned

AlphaEvolve focused on the most common failure: running out of time. About a third of the search's trials hit their time limit, as reported in the evaluator's notes, and AlphaEvolve's best skill is built around that limit.

We also found that running the search is harder than building the loop. After about 10 hours, the search scored no new candidate; our latency check held back every evaluation while model responses were slow, and full agent logs filled the controller's disk. It’s important to plan for slow model windows and for log storage before a long search.

In addition, skills paid off when they added what the agent lacks, as advised by the Agent Skills best practices. Our baseline skill made no measurable difference, while the skill holding the answers added 33 points on the dev tasks.

Our hypothesis: today's models and coding agents are already tuned for coding work, so general advice has little left to add. If so, the room is in specifics, which a search can find: AlphaEvolve's best skill is built around the agent's most common failure, running out of time.

What's next

We’re testing AlphaEvolve on enterprise agent harnesses — system prompt, policy instructions, and tools — where the agent lacks business rules that a search can add. In one small study on customer service test cases for a fictional bank, AlphaEvolve found and fixed a wrong policy rule we had planted, and carried the fix over to cases it never saw.

Other small studies were mixed, and we’ll share our final results when we’ve completed the full study.

Get started

  • AlphaEvolve on Google Cloud: the GitHub repository.

  • Benchmark and harness: Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harbor.

  • Agent skills: the format at agentskills.io and the opencode skills docs.

Thanks for reading! Tell us what your own tests show on LinkedIn or X.

entries.content:
The Google Cloud Data Analytics, BI, and Database teams

Recent product news and updates from our data analytics, database and business intelligence teams.

November 2 - November 6

  • BigQuery observability for data agents is now generally available: Data teams can now monitor the performance, adoption, latency, and cost of BigQuery data agents and their multi-turn conversations using Google Cloud Observability. This capability provides production-grade visibility into agent execution traces, usage volume, and query behavior so organizations can scale conversational analytics with confidence. Review the BigQuery release notes.

  • BigQuery change history and continuous queries for Apache Iceberg managed tables are now GA: BigQuery change history and continuous queries are now generally available for Lakehouse for Apache Iceberg managed tables. You can use the APPENDS table-valued function to track row additions over a specific time range and run continuous queries to read incoming data from and write output rows to Apache Iceberg managed tables. Review the BigQuery release notes.

  • BigQuery Data Engineering Agent adds support for BigQuery AI and ML functions: The BigQuery Data Engineering Agent now supports BigQuery AI, ML, and object functions and statements directly inside generated Dataform SQLX pipelines and agent instruction files. Paired with new folder-based Git repository integration in BigQuery Studio, data engineers can build, version, and automate AI-enriched data pipelines faster. Review the BigQuery release notes.

  • AlloyDB for PostgreSQL introduces AI-powered SQL tuning in preview: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL added the ai.tune_sql function in Public Preview. The function combines AI models with query execution plans and runtime statistics to automatically recommend query rewrites, missing indexes, vacuum operations, and database flag adjustments. Review the AlloyDB release notes.

  • Zero-downtime embedding model upgrades in AlloyDB AI: A new technical guide demonstrates how to upgrade vector embedding models in AlloyDB AI without disrupting production traffic. Using automatic embeddings alongside ScaNN vector indexes, engineering teams can transition to newer embedding models in the background while keeping semantic search and RAG applications online. Read the blog.

  • Shrink Cloud SQL for SQL Server storage disks with minimal downtime using Database Migration Service: A new technical guide demonstrates how to reclaim underutilized storage and reduce infrastructure costs on Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances using Database Migration Service (DMS). This workflow migrates databases to right-sized target disks with continuous replication so teams can downsize over-provisioned storage with minimal cutover downtime. Read the blog.

  • Dataflow Streaming Engine adds latency tiers and scheduled autoscaling: Dataflow introduced new horizontal autoscaling controls for Streaming Engine jobs, allowing teams to select low, medium, or high latency tiers to tune backlog sensitivity. Engineers can also configure recurring autoscaling schedules to adjust minimum and maximum worker counts or utilization targets during predictable traffic windows. Review the Dataflow release notes.

  • Spanner adds ON DELETE SET NULL foreign key actions across GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL: Spanner now supports the ON DELETE SET NULL referential action on foreign keys for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. When a referenced parent row is deleted, Spanner automatically updates the referencing child columns to NULL, simplifying schema migrations and relational integrity management. Review the Spanner release notes.

October 26 - October 30

  • LookML metadata indexing in Knowledge Catalog is now generally available: LookML models, Explores, Views, and join logic now continuously sync into the Knowledge Catalog context graph. This integration provides turnkey grounding for Gemini Enterprise and custom AI agents with deterministic business math, paired with end-to-end lineage tracing from underlying BigQuery tables directly to individual Looker dashboard tiles. Read the announcement blog.

  • Best Buy accelerates self-service insights with conversational analytics in BigQuery: Best Buy deployed conversational data agents directly against BigQuery to empower retail teams with multi-turn natural language exploration. The implementation reduces reliance on manual SQL and dedicated engineering queues, accelerating strategic planning and forecasting cycles while preserving enterprise governance and data protections validated against historical sales records. Explore the Best Buy customer story.

  • Myer accelerates retail insights with BigQuery data agents and Gemini: Leading department store Myer rolled out conversational data agents in BigQuery across 50+ retail analytics projects. Powered by Gemini, the solution enables commercial and merchandising teams to analyze store performance, stock levels, and customer trends using plain English, speeding up decision-making and reducing backlog requests for data teams. Read the Myer case study.

  • Rightmove speeds real estate analytics and predictive forecasting with Looker: The UK's top property portal unified its business analytics on Looker and BigQuery, delivering 4x faster reporting for 400+ team members and cutting meeting prep from hours to minutes. In addition, Rightmove built forecasting models that predict lead volume within 2–4.5% of actual results, while piloting Conversational Analytics in Looker. Read the Rightmove customer story.

  • BigQuery adds AI.TRANSLATE and AI.CHUNK_DOCUMENT for in-database text and RAG pipelines: BigQuery introduced two native generative AI capabilities to simplify unstructured data workflows directly within SQL. The 

    AI.TRANSLATE
    function enables multilingual translation across Neural Machine Translation and Translation LLMs, while the 
    AI.CHUNK_DOCUMENT
    table-valued function partitions unstructured text into semantically coherent segments optimized for vector embeddings and RAG pipelines. Review the BigQuery release notes.

  • AlloyDB adds in-database ai.extract and ai.classify functions to accelerate operational AI: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL introduced two new AI functions, 

    ai.extract
    and 
    ai.classify,
    in Public Preview, allowing developers to extract structured entities and categorize unstructured text directly inside SQL queries without external inference pipelines. These functions add to existing AlloyDB AI capabilities such as summarizing, generating, and filtering data with AI. Review the AlloyDB release notes.

  • AlloyDB Omni Web UI is generally available for centralized hybrid database management: The AlloyDB Omni Web UI is now generally available, providing a centralized graphical interface to manage hybrid and on-premises PostgreSQL deployments. Database administrators can monitor multi-cluster topologies, inspect columnar engine metrics, diagnose slow queries with Query Insights, and verify AI model connectivity across their database fleet. Review the AlloyDB Omni release notes.

  • Cloud Spanner adds approximate aggregate functions for high-speed analytics at scale: Cloud Spanner now supports approximate aggregate functions across both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. Powered by HyperLogLog++ sketches, these functions generate fast statistical estimates for distinct count metrics with minimal compute overhead, accelerating analytical queries and reporting dashboards across petabyte-scale operational datasets. Review the Cloud Spanner release notes.

  • Knowledge Catalog introduces self-learning context enrichment and Knowledge Studio (Preview): Knowledge Catalog's enrichment agent now learns from agent and user interactions and from sources such as playbooks, code repositories, and business documents to find and fix missing or outdated context, which teams can package into reusable context sets. Knowledge Studio, the new studio experience in Knowledge Catalog, lets context engineers and data stewards explore their data estate conversationally, navigate a visual context graph, and review changes before they reach users and agents. Based on internal benchmarks, grounding agents in Knowledge Catalog makes them nearly 4x more accurate, with up to 33% lower latency and using up to 75% fewer tokens. Read the launch blog.

  • Knowledge Catalog now grounds AI agents in the semantic models you already trust (GA): Knowledge Catalog natively ingests semantic models and metric definitions from Looker LookML, BigQuery Graph, dbt MetricFlow, Snowflake Semantic Views, Databricks Metric Views, and SAP Core Schema Notation, and connects them with lineage, data quality, and access controls in a single context graph. Gemini Enterprise, BigQuery conversational analytics, and custom agents retrieve a metric's trusted formula, verified join path, and backing table in one context call, without moving data or rewriting business logic. Read the launch blog.

October 19 - October 23

  • BigQuery introduces column aliases in GoogleSQL and cross-region table copy GA

    GoogleSQL in BigQuery now supports column aliases in 

    SELECT
    and 
    WHERE
    clauses (GA opt-in), avoiding nested subqueries and simplifying migrations from Snowflake and Teradata. Cross-region table copying is also now generally available to streamline regional data replication and disaster recovery. Review the BigQuery release notes.

  • Conversational analytics in BigQuery expands to Canada and adds CSV/PDF export

    Conversational analytics in BigQuery is now available in Montréal (

    northamerica-northeast1
    ) and Toronto (
    northamerica-northeast2
    ) to support Canadian data residency requirements. You can also now export agent responses — including text, tables, charts, and citations — directly to CSV or PDF (GA). Learn more about conversational analytics in BigQuery.

  • AlloyDB Omni 18.4.0 is now GA with Advanced Query Insights and external KMS support

    AlloyDB Omni 18.4.0 brings PostgreSQL 18.4 to self-hosted and multi-cloud environments, adding the 

    google_insights_v2
    extension for granular query execution and wait-event diagnostics. It also adds Thales CipherTrust Manager support for Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) alongside HashiCorp Vault. Explore the AlloyDB Omni release notes.

  • Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL adds managed connection pooling and Private Service Connect defaults

    Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL now supports enabling built-in managed connection pooling on existing Private Service Connect (PSC) instances to scale high-concurrency workloads. PSC is also now the default private IP option for new Cloud SQL instances in new projects to simplify cross-project networking. Review Cloud SQL updates.

  • Customer momentum: Unico prevents over $5B in fraud on Google's Agentic Data Cloud

    Digital identity platform Unico migrated from Databricks Spark/Scala clusters to BigQuery and Spanner at the core of its data architecture. Unifying real-time transaction streams with petabyte-scale analytics enabled low-latency identity verification that has prevented over $5 billion in fraud. Read the Unico case study.

  • Developer guide: Getting started with Looker Data Apps

    Following the debut of Looker Data Apps in preview, a new walkthrough on the Google Developer Community shares practical patterns for building prompt-driven applications inside Looker. Read the guide on the Google Developer Community.

October 12 - October 16

  • Looker Data Apps are now in Preview to build and host interactive, agent-generated applications natively inside Looker

    Generated using natural language prompts, the Antigravity CLI, or Claude Code, these interactive web applications, natively hosted inside Looker, transform business reporting into operational systems of action. Users can test scenarios, adjust parameters, and trigger workflows in downstream platforms while inheriting LookML semantic modeling, row-level security, and access controls with no runtime LLM token costs. Read the announcement blog.

  • Build end-to-end data science pipelines with the Data Agent Kit

    Following the general availability of the Data Agent Kit, a new end-to-end walkthrough demonstrates how data teams can build, test, and schedule machine learning pipelines directly from their preferred code editors. Explore the walkthrough and codelab.

  • Manage dashboard agents as code to bring CI/CD and version control to LookML dashboards

    Data teams can now declare agent parameters, configurations, and prompt instructions alongside dashboard files in code. This integration enables standard developer workflows for conversational BI, including Git version control, peer review, branching, and automated CI/CD validation before agent modifications reach production end users. Read the technical guide on the Google Developer Community.

  • Simplify AI search with native AlloyDB hybrid search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion

    AlloyDB for PostgreSQL simplifies hybrid search architectures by combining vector similarity search and keyword BM25 retrieval within a unified database engine. Using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), developers can merge lexical scoring and semantic embeddings into a single ranked result without writing a complex SQL query. This unified approach removes the operational overhead of running and synchronizing external search engines alongside operational databases for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and search applications.Explore hybrid search in AlloyDB.

October 5 - October 9

  • Data Agent Kit is now generally available to bring Google Data Cloud to any coding agent

    Data Agent Kit provides a free collection of Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and Google-authored agent skills that connect more than 15 Google Data Cloud services directly to coding agents across VS Code, Antigravity, Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. This release expands support for developers and data practitioners to inspect schemas, author queries, and build end-to-end data pipelines in natural language directly from their IDE or CLI. Read the announcement blog.

  • Spanner Omni is now generally available for deploy-anywhere, multi-model workloads

    Spanner Omni brings Spanner's distributed SQL, graph, vector, and key-value capabilities to any environment, including on-premises data centers, other public clouds via Kubernetes or VMs, and local developer laptops. Organizations can build and run multi-model applications with consistent APIs and query engines across hybrid and multi-cloud footprints while seamlessly scaling to managed Spanner on Google Cloud. Read the launch blog and explore how Spanner also removed cumulative mutation limits for DML transactions.

  • AlloyDB delivers PostgreSQL for agents and native BM25 hybrid search

    We announced PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB, introducing an agentic database architecture engineered for real-time data access at agent scale with workload isolation. In addition, native BM25 ranking is now in Preview for AlloyDB and Cloud SQL, allowing developers to combine keyword search and vector embeddings directly in PostgreSQL without maintaining an external search engine. For hybrid deployments, the AlloyDB Omni RPM Orchestrator is now generally available, and you can dive deeper in our new Build AI apps and agents with AlloyDB eBook.

  • Lakehouse runtime catalog adds regional endpoints across 22 regions and GA support for flexible column names

    Lakehouse runtime catalog regional endpoints are now live across 22 Google Cloud regions across the Americas, Europe, Asia-Pacific, and the Middle East, supporting both the Apache Iceberg REST catalog endpoint and the Apache Hive catalog endpoint to help customers meet strict data residency and sovereignty requirements. In addition, flexible column names for Apache Iceberg tables are now generally available by default across Iceberg external tables and managed tables, enabling seamless querying of columns containing spaces, hyphens, and Unicode characters. We also announced the Preview of cross-cloud caching and connections for the borderless Lakehouse.

  • Unlock predictive and agent-ready insights with BigQuery augmented analytics TVFs, TabFM, and identity columns

    BigQuery introduced augmented analytics table-valued functions (TVFs): six built-in functions that automate metric diagnostics, trend analysis, and pattern discovery directly where your data lives and integrate as skills for AI agents. We also introduced TabFM in BigQuery to bring tabular foundation model capabilities to predictive analytics, alongside BigQuery identity columns to automatically generate sequential surrogate keys and simplify data warehouse pipelines.

  • Dataflow adds Pause/Resume and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU support for large-scale AI workloads

    New Dataflow capabilities make it easier to run high-throughput streaming and batch AI pipelines at scale, including Pause/Resume job controls and support for NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. And for teams running Apache Spark workloads, learn how to mitigate compute stockouts and maximize availability using flexible VMs.

  • Unlock up to 3x higher QPS and microsecond latency with Memorystore for Valkey 9.1

    Memorystore for Valkey 9.1 is now available, delivering up to 3x higher queries per second (QPS) and microsecond-level caching latencies to accelerate high-throughput applications and real-time AI agent state management. Read the blog.

  • Customer momentum across Google Data Cloud — Yahoo, PayPal, Surescripts, Airwallex, and Lucius AI

    Organizations across industries are scaling their data and AI foundations on Google Data Cloud. Yahoo uses flexible VMs in Managed Service for Apache Spark to reduce provisioning failures by 85%, while PayPal migrated mission-critical analytics workloads to Managed Service for Apache Spark to scale and reduce operational overhead. On the database front, Surescripts migrated 30.5 billion annual healthcare transactions to AlloyDB with 99.998% uptime, Airwallex manages more than 5,000 databases with 99.99% availability on Cloud SQL with a team of four DBAs, and Lucius AI runs a 210,000-tender global platform on AlloyDB and MCP with 47x faster ScaNN vector search.

September 7 - September 10

  • Pub/Sub SMTs can now AI Inference your Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform models!

    Pub/Sub AI Inference SMTs allow you to apply inference on an incoming stream of events using models hosted in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The model’s prediction is appended to your event, making it available for downstream processing in your data warehouse (like BigQuery) or operational database (like BigTable). This feature, now generally available, can dramatically simplify or enhance anomaly detection systems you are operating. 

  • PostgreSQL Source Connector is now generally available in Managed Service for Apache Kafka!

    Managed Service for Apache Kafka’s PostgreSQL connector allows customers to capture changes from their PostgreSQL database and ingest them into their Kafka infrastructure with low latency. This source connector is compatible withCloud SQL for Postgres, AlloyDB, and self-managed PostgreSQL databases. Try this along with our entire portfolio of managed connectors, including MirrorMaker 2.0, BigQuery, Cloud Storage, and Pub/Sub! E-mail kafka-hotline@google.com if you have questions or feedback!

  • Pause-on-failure for Dataflow batch jobs is GA

    Dataflow pause-on-failure enables you to preserve the state of a batch Dataflow job before it fails. By pausing your Dataflow job, you can address issues that are external to the pipeline and resume processing without losing completed work. This helps you better manage resource costs and improve job reliability when you face temporary outages or capacity constraints.

  • The insertAll API is now the BigQuery Storage Write API (REST)

    The legacy insertAll streaming API is now rebranded as the BigQuery Storage Write API (REST). By dropping the "legacy" label, developers can confidently build long-term HTTP-based streaming workflows. This stateless JSON-over-HTTPS endpoint offers a lightweight alternative to heavy gRPC libraries—ideal for serverless web apps, IoT telemetry, and AI logging. The transition is seamless for existing users, requiring zero code changes and offering 100% backward compatibility. However, the Storage Write API (gRPC) version remains the recommended standard for high-throughput, continuous pipelines.

August 31 - September 4

  • Stateful processing is available in BigQuery continuous queries in Preview

    Stateful operations significantly expand what’s possible with BigQuery continuous queries. This feature allows users to leverage functions like 
    JOIN
    s, aggregations, and windowing functions directly in their streaming queries. Now you can calculate metrics over time (for example, a 30-minute average) to power your downstream applications and AI agents with much richer, real-time signals.

    Try out our featurehere and share your feedback with bq-continuous-queries-feedback@google.com!

  • Synthetic data generator tool is available for Managed Service for Kafka

    You’ve launched your first Kafka cluster. Now what? The next thing to do is to produce some data to the cluster, but that involves modifying a client application somewhere or spinning up a virtual machine. The synthetic data generator tool, now generally available, can start sending mock data to your cluster in 3 clicks, and will get data streaming into your cluster in less than two minutes. The perfect utility for those moments you just want to test your cluster and new features. Try our quickstart today!

  • Dataflow pipeline updates are faster & more flexible

entries.title: Powering open infrastructure for autonomous agents
entries.summary: As AI shifts from human scale to agent scale, from systems of record to systems of action, and from simple requests to complex agentic workflows, the workload underneath your platform changes completely. An agent works in a continuous, stateful loop: It proposes an action, spins up subagents, executes code or tool calls inside a sandbox, and feeds the results back into the model for the next turn.
entries.content:
Drew Bradstock

VP Product Management, Orchestration & Kubernetes

Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL have been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox; Agent Substrate has reached 1.0, and is GA on GKE

As AI shifts from human scale to agent scale, from systems of record to systems of action, and from simple requests to complex agentic workflows, the workload underneath your platform changes completely. An agent works in a continuous, stateful loop: It proposes an action, spins up subagents, executes code or tool calls inside a sandbox, and feeds the results back into the model for the next turn. Running that loop at scale requires the same open foundation and neutral governance that Kubernetes and the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) brought to containers in the 2010s.

Today, we are announcing the donation of Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL, three open source projects that started at Google, to the CNCF following their acceptance last month into the CNCF Sandbox. To bring this open stack into managed production and accelerate it across TPUs and GPUs, we are also announcing that Agent Substrate has reached its 1.0 milestone and is now generally available as Agent Substrate on GKE.

Each project is now working through CNCF Sandbox onboarding with community maintainers and independent build infrastructure, and gVisor is on a path toward Incubation. These releases deliver an open stack that runs on any Kubernetes cluster, on any cloud, across CPUs, GPUs, or TPUs, by:

  • Scaling isolated agent environments without idle compute overhead with Agent Substrate (now 1.0 and GA on GKE): Agents execute code or tests for a few seconds, then wait on model turns, external APIs, or human input. Keeping a dedicated container alive during those pauses ties up memory and compute. Agent Substrate decouples stateful agent sessions and identities from active compute, snapshotting idle agents to storage and restoring them in under 500 milliseconds to run millions of sandboxes at 10x container density.

  • Isolating untrusted code within a sandbox with gVisor: Agents routinely generate and run unreviewed code and external packages, making standard containers that share a host Linux kernel a security risk. gVisor isolates generated code inside a lightweight userspace application kernel at container packing density on any Linux node.

  • Distributing post training and serving efficiently with OpenRL: Training agents with reinforcement learning (RL) gives builders an open loop to learn across millions of parallel sandboxed rollouts. OpenRL orchestrates self-hosted RL post-training loops in plain Python on Kubernetes.

Scale fully isolated agent environments with Substrate

Agents need isolated compute resources and strict access boundaries, yet spend most of their time waiting: executing code for a few seconds, then pausing while a model reasons or a human responds. They need a discrete identity and central enforcement point to ensure the agent only accesses authorized tools and services without holding sensitive keys. In standard Kubernetes, giving every active agent its own Pod locks up memory and CPU while the agent sits idle, forces the control plane to track millions of persistent objects it was never designed to hold, and ties identities directly to Pods. At the same time, identities are intrinsically tied to Kubernetes Pods, adding exponential complexity for controlling access and secrets.

Agent Substrate solves this by separating the stateful agent from the underlying compute:

  • Actors hold each agent's memory, files, and discrete identity.

  • Workers are reusable execution sandboxes drawn from a warm Kubernetes pool.

  • Gateways enforce inbound and outbound access control and inject secrets based on Actor identity, keeping sensitive keys out of the agent environment.

When an agent pauses to wait on a model turn or tool call, Agent Substrate snapshots the agent’s memory and files to storage and immediately returns the Worker to the warm pool. When the next request arrives, Agent Substrate restores the Actor onto any available Worker in under 500 milliseconds and picks up right where it left off. Think of it as a hotel room rather than a house: you don't keep a room when you leave town, and a new room is ready when you come back.

Agent Substrate decouples stateful Actors and policy Gateways from a warm pool of Kubernetes Workers, restoring idle sessions in under 500 milliseconds.

Since public development started in May 2026, the Agent Substrate project has grown to more than 100 contributors. Early design partners like Nous Research are building Hermes Enterprise on it, and it already powers other CNCF projects like kagent.

Further, reaching the 1.0 milestone shows that Agent Substrate can accept production workloads across millions of sandboxes, achieving 10x the density of standard container runtimes, and performing more than 500 suspend and resume activations per second.

Underneath, you can choose Cloud Hypervisor microVMs or gVisor as your isolation boundary without changing how you manage agent lifecycles. Because Agent Substrate runs standard OCI containers, it works out of the box with Agent Development Kit (ADK) agents, stateful coding environments, and productivity agents.

With today's general availability of Agent Substrate on GKE, you can run this runtime as a managed capability on Google Cloud or deploy the open-source code on any Kubernetes cluster. For teams that want a dedicated microVM compute service through an API without having to manage clusters, Agent Substrate complements Agent Compute Engine, our Titanium microVM service that features fast hibernation and parallel environment-forking for evaluation and RL pipelines.

SPIRITT is building their SPIRITT Workspace, a platform where agents run real work autonomously while humans collaborate to steer the vision, on top of Agent Substrate on GKE. 

”At SPIRITT, every customer gets an autonomous AI workspace where an agent, or a whole swarm of agents, builds, runs, and ships real work across the organization, from code and development cycles to marketing and operations. Agent Substrate on GKE gives us the security isolation to let agents execute code safely, the extensibility to plug in our own runtime, and the density to run every customer's agents economically at scale." - Tamir Magen, CEO, SPIRITT

Isolate untrusted agent code with gVisor

When agents shift from systems of record to systems of action, they run generated shell commands and unreviewed packages. Standard containers share the host Linux kernel with every other workload on the node, which is a risky bet for untrusted code. Hardware microVMs offer a strong boundary, and Agent Substrate supports them natively. Many teams also need strong isolation that runs at container density across any standard Linux instance, even when bare metal or nested virtualization isn't available.

gVisor provides that isolation through a lightweight application kernel written in Go. Sitting between the container and the host OS, gVisor intercepts and handles application system calls in userspace so untrusted code never talks directly to the host kernel. Open sourced by Google in 2018, gVisor runs millions of sandboxes every day underneath GKE Sandbox and Cloud Run. Outside Google, Anthropic and OpenAI use it to contain code execution, Modal and Snowflake run their execution sandboxes on it, and Ant Group and Tencent run it in production at scale.

Three capabilities make gVisor a natural fit for agent fleets:

  • Container density and flexible memory: Unlike VMs that preallocate fixed blocks of RAM, gVisor keeps a container process model where memory scales up and down with the workload, packing more agents onto every node and lowering your cost per agent.

  • Native GPU, TPU, and snapshot support: gVisor supports GPUs, TPUs, and checkpoint/restore natively, so agents can access accelerators inside the sandbox and pause when idle.

  • Runs anywhere Linux runs: Because it doesn't require nested virtualization, gVisor deploys identically across any cloud or local Linux node. Northflank, for example, uses gVisor to sandbox GPU workloads when nested virtualization isn't available.

Donating gVisor to the CNCF clears a longstanding performance barrier for the community. Sandboxed infrastructure providers, including Google, all carry host kernel patches that bring gVisor's I/O performance close to that of native Linux, but upstream Linux maintainers declined to merge them while the project was owned by a single vendor. Moving to neutral CNCF governance opens the path to upstreaming those kernel optimizations, so every builder gets near native performance out of the box. With this move, Ant Group, Modal, and Tines have committed to join gVisor's maintainers, with OpenAI, Tencent, and NVIDIA continuing their contributions.

Scale RL post training on Kubernetes with OpenRL

The sandbox that runs your agent in production is the exact same environment you need to train an agent with reinforcement learning. Today, most frontier capability gains come from RL post-training: running millions of multiturn rollouts inside real tools, scoring the outcomes, and updating model weights. Building that loop yourself usually means forking a monolithic RL framework and debugging distributed weight transfers before you ever touch your training algorithm.

OpenRL brings a clean, self-hosted Python post-training loop directly to your Kubernetes cluster, with:

  • Simple Python primitives: Write your training loop using four clean primitives (

    sample
    , 
    forward_backward
    , 
    optim_step
    , and 
    save_state
    ) through a Tinker compatible API while keeping your weights and data on your own cluster. Existing 
    tinker-cookbook
    recipes run unchanged, supporting both LoRA adapters and full parameter fine-tuning.

  • Pluggable engines and Kubernetes scheduling: OpenRL uses Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) to partition your accelerator pool and orchestrate RL work on the shared pool. Its pluggable architecture uses standard engines, including 

    PyTorch
    /
    AutoModel
    for training and 
    vLLM
    for sampling, with Gemma and Qwen validated out of the box, and with TPU support on the roadmap.

OpenRL also pairs with llm-d, the CNCF distributed inference and RL project founded by Red Hat, Google Cloud, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA that recently reached 1.0, to keep your accelerators busy across both phases of RL. Here, llm-d provides:

  • Prefix-aware rollout routing: The llm-d router routes multiturn rollouts to samplers that already hold matching KV cache prefixes, cutting redundant prefill compute.

  • GPU time-slicing between training and sampling: In RL training, samplers and trainers take turns, leaving one set of chips idle while the other works. OpenRL uses llm-d time-slicing to share the same physical GPUs between sampling and training, reclaiming idle accelerator cycles the same way Agent Substrate reclaims idle CPU and RAM.

OpenRL drives plain Python RL loops on Kubernetes, running episodes inside Agent Substrate sandboxes while llm-d routes rollouts and time slices accelerators.

OpenRL is the newest layer of this stack by a wide margin. It started in February as a research preview, and we are bringing it to the CNCF early on purpose. Its north star is one recipe for any model on any accelerator, and no single company can get there alone. To get there, you need the people building accelerators (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and TPUs), inference engines (

llm-d
, 
vLLM
, 
SGLang
), training frameworks, and open-weight models starting with Gemma and Qwen. Setting up neutral CNCF governance before the design hardens makes room for everyone to build it together.

Why the CNCF, and why now

Improving the security and efficiency of AI agents takes joint design across the runtime, scheduler, compiler, and silicon. The past year made the need for affordable, isolated sandboxing and open post-training infrastructure exceedingly clear. Donating Agent Substrate, gVisor, and OpenRL to the CNCF reaffirms Google’s commitment to open collaboration and co-investment. Vendor-neutral ownership lets cloud providers, hardware vendors, and independent software companies participate in the future growth of agentic workloads equally.

We believe that these donations will accelerate the development and adoption of agentic workloads through these projects similarly to what we saw with Kubernetes.

Come find us at KubeCon

Join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City (November 9 to 12) across our sessions and at the Google Cloud booth to learn more about Agent Substrate, OpenRL, and gVisor. You will also hear soon from community partners including Modal, Anyscale, and Tecton on what this open stack means for their agentic workloads. In the meantime, here is where to start:

  • Follow the CNCF Sandbox applications: gVisor #521, Agent Substrate #523, and OpenRL #518, alongside cohort peer KubeRay #525

  • Kick the tires: ate.dev, gvisor.dev, and openrl.dev 

  • Run agents on GKE today: Agent Substrate on GKE, and GKE Sandbox

  • Read the deep dives: Agent Substrate on GKE, gVisor's move to the CNCF, and Introducing OpenRL
